text: Build on the context graph and catalogs you already maintain. Give agents shared memory that learns from outcomes, with versioned context for evaluation and training. For Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, Cursor and Copilot. Versioned memory Your existing context, connected to agent experience. How context becomes agent experience. Illustrative memory version. Memory shaped to your goals, improved by experience and grounded in the context your company already maintains. This is AmpUp's assessment, based on the evaluations and named baselines below. Broader leaderboard standing has not been independently verified. In our evaluations, root-cause accuracy on ORCA-bench rose from 6.3% to 35.2%, and CRM question accuracy on CRMArena-Pro rose from 57.6% to 76.7%. Explore six public benchmarks and two internal evaluations below. ORCA-bench, 253 incident tasks, Haiku 5.5. Each point is scored on days the notes didn't learn from. After day 3 of graded practice Enterprise Brain 35.2 % of tasks solved No memory 6.3% Graded runs 454 learned from so far * Code review's interval is 98.3%, corrected for several comparisons. All other intervals are 95%. Store agent memory and trajectory records in the same cloud storage. Each record is pinned to a memory version. Use those records to evaluate system performance through the control plane and train custom models. Through your control plane From the same pinned records One shared destination for memory, evaluation and training. Illustrative trajectory and evaluation view. Each record keeps its memory version. Store memory and pinned trajectory records together. Understand how the system is doing through the control plane. Use the same records with their original memory context. A trajectory connects the task, the memory version, the steps taken and the outcome. Keep that context with each record as you prepare evaluation and training datasets. Memory sits in open Apache Iceberg tables and moves through the engine as Apache Arrow. Training jobs can read a pinned snapshot while agents keep writing. $ memstore workspace snapshot orca_goal $ memstore train-log export <scope> --out FILE In our benchmarks, every Enterprise Brain arm on ORCA-bench (4), τ²-bench banking (4) and SWE-ContextBench (2) read one content-hashed memory version, recorded with every attempt it scored. The benchmark results above measure learned memory and guidance. We haven’t trained a model from these tables yet. For a long-running task, an agent works on its own branch and records memories as it goes. When the run completes, those memories merge into mainline. Collect memories during the run. Share them after it completes. Illustrative memory entries and version numbers. Give the agent its own memory during the run. Record useful context as the agent progresses. Merge the completed run’s memories into mainline. Your team can also use branches to try a schema or compile guidance before changing mainline. Pin a snapshot for evaluation; conflicting merges are refused. $ memstore workspace branch orca_goal oncall $ memstore compile team:acme/support --branch arm1 $ memstore workspace snapshot orca_goal --branch oncall merge · three-way In the engine's model test, 100 random sequences of 15 operations matched the reference model: 204 merges, 26 refused as conflicts. Start on a laptop, then deploy in your own cloud account. AWS and Google Cloud are ready. LAPTOP Try it locally. Memory stays on your machine; only model calls leave it. SNOWFLAKE Keep memory in your Snowflake account, stored as open Iceberg tables. GOOGLE CLOUD (GCP) Ready. Store memory in your own catalog and bucket. AWS Ready. Deploy Enterprise Brain in your own AWS account. Databricks is not yet available. Manage sign-in, team access, connected sources and deployments in one place. The control plane holds none of your memory. ENTERPRISE CONTROLS Your deployment sends only approved operational telemetry to the control plane. Facts, queries and organization names are rejected. Wherever the server runs. On a laptop it stays under ~/.memstore . In Snowflake nothing is sent to AmpUp. On Google Cloud, setup scripts put the tables in your catalog and bucket. During the preview a team can also use a server AmpUp runs, and then AmpUp stores that team's memory. Model calls go through OpenRouter by default; a direct backend can keep them inside your cloud. Mem0 and vector databases are generic memory: they store what was said and find it again, the same way for everyone. On that job alone, Mem0 open source and Enterprise Brain tie on LongMemEval (82.2% vs 79.7%). Enterprise Brain is built to learn: it extracts the facts your goals call for, in your vertical's schema, and rewrites a note for each kind of task from your graded runs. Permissions carry over from every source, and the memory sits in Iceberg tables in your own catalog. A CLAUDE.md file holds rules you already know; notes capture the ones you don't yet. It depends on the task. On ORCA-bench, notes from 135 runs scored 16.2%, from 284 runs 19.8% and from 454 runs 35.2%, against 6.3% with no memory. The DolphinBench note above came from six runs. On τ²-bench, notes showed no measurable gain. Search and saved memory work from the first session. An agent that writes memory mid-task sees only its own session, and it has a task to finish. Dreaming runs out of band with its own budget and sees what the whole team's agents have written. It ends values a newer fact replaced, links two facts that say the same thing, and joins the names of one thing ( owner and maintained_by , rep memory and rep memory page). It only adds rows, so as_of still reads what was there before. It runs for one audience at a time, so it never mixes in facts a reader couldn't see. A dry run prints every decision with the model's reason, and one command takes back everything a pass did. It is off by default; turn it on per org or team, and it runs nightly or hourly. On Snowflake or Google Cloud it is Iceberg tables in your own catalog, readable by Snowflake and BigQuery, so it stays with you. On a laptop it stays on disk. On AmpUp's preview server, AmpUp stores it. When a whole history fits and the model reads it well, reading it all wins (93.0% vs 58–61% with Haiku on LongMemEval). Mem0 leads on time-based questions. Compiled procedures alone, before any graded runs, scored below plain files on τ²-bench (21.0% vs 27.8%). Sonnet 5.5 beat Haiku with notes on SWE-ContextBench by about 5 points, and on DolphinBench by 9.2 when Sonnet read the history as files. On code review, learned notes didn't help, though evidence from past work did; on alert triage, memory hasn't helped yet. Claude Opus 5.5 for the rare steps whose output every later task reads: compiling procedures and writing notes. Claude Haiku 5.5 for extraction, judging and routing. Each is configurable per org.
